stem: Explain why some human rights may be limited, giving **three** examples.

points.description: Identifies an example (e.g. expression limited to prevent hate speech).
Explains: protects the rights/dignity of others.
Identifies an example (e.g. movement or assembly limited in an epidemic).
Explains: protects public health/safety.
Identifies an example (e.g. liberty removed after conviction).
Explains: prevents crime / enforces the law; limits must be fair, reasonable and necessary.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Freedom of expression may be limited to stop hate speech or false statements, because these damage the rights and dignity of others. Freedom of movement and assembly may be limited during an epidemic to protect public health. The right to liberty is limited when a court sends a convicted person to prison, to prevent crime. Such limits are allowed only when they are fair, reasonable and necessary in a democratic society.

hints: For each example, say whose interests the limit protects.

stem: Assess the government's efforts to promote children's rights in Zimbabwe.

points.description: Effort: constitutional protection of children's rights; ratification of the CRC.
Effort: expansion of education after 1980 / help with fees for vulnerable children.
Effort: immunisation and child health programmes; 2016 ruling against child marriage.
Limit: economic problems restrict free education and health care.
Limit: child marriage, child labour and gaps in birth registration persist in some areas.
Supported judgement.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The government has done much on paper and in practice. The Constitution protects children's rights, and Zimbabwe ratified the CRC in 1990. Education expanded rapidly after 1980, and vulnerable children have been helped with fees. Immunisation campaigns improved child health, and in 2016 the Constitutional Court ruled that no one may marry before 18. However, economic difficulties have made free education and health care hard to provide for all, and child marriage, child labour and gaps in birth registration persist in some areas. Overall the legal framework is strong, but the rights are not yet fully enjoyed in practice.

explanation: One mark per point, including the judgement.
hints: Give efforts and limits, then judge.

stem:
Study the source and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a report by a fictional district child protection committee in Matabeleland North, 2019 (invented for this question)

> This year 64 children were helped to obtain birth certificates, and two girls aged 15 were returned to school after their planned marriages were stopped. However, many families cannot afford school fees, and some children herd cattle or work in gardens during school hours. The clinic reports good immunisation rates.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Identify **three** achievements reported in Source A.

points.description: Children helped to obtain birth certificates.
Planned child marriages stopped / girls returned to school.
Good immunisation rates.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which children's rights does the report suggest are not fully protected? Explain your answer.

points.description: Right to education (families cannot afford fees).
Right to protection from child labour (herding cattle during school hours).
Explanation linking poverty to these problems.

parts.explanation: Rights linked to evidence in the source.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How far does Source A show that government efforts to protect children's rights have been successful? Use the source and your own knowledge.

points.description: Success shown: birth registration and stopping child marriage (fits 2016 ruling).
Success shown: immunisation (fits national programmes with UNICEF/WHO).
Limits shown: fees and child labour.
Own knowledge: economic problems limit free education and health care nationally.
Provenance: one district; a committee may stress its own achievements.
Supported judgement.

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The source shows some success. Children were helped to get birth certificates, two child marriages were stopped, in line with the Constitutional Court's 2016 ruling, and immunisation rates were good, which fits national immunisation programmes run with UNICEF and the WHO.

But it also shows limits: many families cannot pay school fees, and some children work during school hours, so the rights to education and to protection from child labour are not fully enjoyed. From my own knowledge, economic problems have made free education and health care hard to provide across the country.

The report covers one district, and a committee may stress its own achievements. Overall it shows partial success: legal protection and some services work, but poverty limits children's rights in practice.

explanation: Source-based practice question on children's rights (12 marks).
hints: Separate achievements from problems, then test the report against your own knowledge.

points.description: Respect parents, elders and teachers.
Attend school and work hard.
Respect the rights of others (no bullying).
Obey the law / care for health and environment / help in the community.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far does the Constitution of Zimbabwe go beyond the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in protecting rights?

points.description: Similar: both list civil and political rights (life, liberty, expression, fair trial, vote).
Similar: both list social rights (education, health, standard of living).
Beyond: the Constitution is binding law enforceable in courts; the UDHR is a declaration.
Beyond: specific groups (children, women, elderly, disabled, veterans), environmental rights, limitation rules and the ZHRC.
Supported judgement.

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The two documents protect many of the same rights. Both include civil and political rights such as life, liberty, freedom of expression, a fair trial and the right to vote, and both include social rights such as education, health and an adequate standard of living. The Constitution's Declaration of Rights clearly draws on the tradition the UDHR began in 1948.

In several ways the Constitution goes further. It is binding law: a person can go to court, including the Constitutional Court, to enforce it, whereas the UDHR is a declaration. It has detailed sections for children, women, the elderly, persons with disabilities and veterans, environmental rights, and rules on when rights may be limited. It also sets up the Zimbabwe Human Rights Commission.

Overall the Constitution goes well beyond the UDHR in enforceability and detail, though how fully its rights are enjoyed depends on resources and enforcement.

hints: In (b), compare the two documents point by point.
